- Geomorphologist Petra Varadi installed erosion markers at 30 stations along a six-kilometer coastal footpath and resurveyed them for four years.
- Standard exposure models predicted the open headland segment would retreat about 16 centimeters per year.
- Markers recorded 11 centimeters of annual retreat on the headland but 24 centimeters in the sheltered cove.
- Varadi attributes the cove's losses to winter frost heave in the cove's clay soils.
- Wave energy and sediment type were logged at every station.
prompt: The student wants to explain why the finding surprised researchers. Which choice most effectively accomplishes this goal?
choices: Varadi expected the exposed headland to retreat about 14 centimeters a year, yet it lost only 9 while the sheltered cove lost 21, a reversal she traces to runoff from a resurfaced car park.

Varadi expected the exposed headland to retreat about 16 centimeters a year, yet it lost only 11 while the sheltered cove lost 24, a reversal she traces to winter frost heave in the cove's clay soils.
Varadi expected the exposed headland to retreat about 12 centimeters a year, yet it lost only 8 while the sheltered cove lost 18, a reversal she traces to burrowing by a colony of sand martins.

Varadi expected the exposed headland to retreat about 18 centimeters a year, yet it lost only 13 while the sheltered cove lost 28, a reversal she traces to foot traffic diverted by a boardwalk closure.
correct_answer: Varadi expected the exposed headland to retreat about 16 centimeters a year, yet it lost only 11 while the sheltered cove lost 24, a reversal she traces to winter frost heave in the cove's clay soils.

- Dr. Nadia Oyelaran audited all 26 public clocks in Harbury, a town of 12,000 residents.
- Each clock's displayed time was compared against a satellite time signal twice daily for one year.
- The clocks include pendulum, electric-synchronous, and quartz mechanisms, all serviced by town custodians.
- Across the year, the median clock drifted 92 seconds fast per week.
- Of the factors Oyelaran tracked, vibration from passing heavy traffic best predicted a clock's drift.

choices: Oyelaran's audit found that Harbury's public clocks drifted a median of 63 seconds slow per week, with the age of the mechanism the strongest predictor of a clock's drift.

Oyelaran's audit found that Harbury's public clocks drifted a median of 47 seconds fast per week, with enclosure temperature swings the strongest predictor of a clock's drift.
Oyelaran's audit found that Harbury's public clocks drifted a median of 38 seconds slow per week, with irregular manual resetting by custodians the strongest predictor of a clock's drift.
correct_answer: Oyelaran's audit found that Harbury's public clocks drifted a median of 92 seconds fast per week, with vibration from passing heavy traffic the strongest predictor of a clock's drift.
